document.title: Ambassador Dean Cable to Secretary of State. Subject: Meeting with Prime Minister Gandhi, June 3
document.authors: Ambassador John Gunther Dean, U.S. Embassy New Delhi
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), A New Phase in the Great Game: U.S., Soviets, India, Pakistan vied to shape a new Afghanistan in late 1980s | National Security Archive
document.note: 50-minute conversation in which Gandhi criticizes Zia's dismissal of Junejo, argues U.S. arms to Pakistan lack a basis after Soviet withdrawal, and says India backs Najibullah only to keep extremists like Hekmatyar from power. He asks whether Pakistan's nuclear progress is an Islamic nuclear force and discusses AWACS.

events.description: Ambassador Dean meets PM Rajiv Gandhi for 50 minutes; Ronen Sen attends.
Zia dismisses Junejo government in Pakistan.
Gorbachev publicly announces Soviet troop withdrawal from Afghanistan.
Ambassador Dean met PM Rajiv Gandhi; Gandhi said India has not decided on a Soviet AWACS and would act only if Pakistan buys a US AWACS.
Gandhi said an American offer to manufacture the F-5 trainer in India would be considered equally, depending on balance-of-payments impact.

Gandhi noted that the purchase of the first US supercomputer was finalized, with shipment scheduled for fall 1988, and asked for negotiations on a second for the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore.
Gandhi planned to travel abroad, returning sometime after June 12, after which he would see Dean.
Ambassador Dean met PM Rajiv Gandhi for 50 minutes, with Ronen Sen present.
Gandhi scheduled to leave for Syria, West Germany, the UN in New York and Hungary, returning June 12.
Zia dismissed Prime Minister Junejo's government at the end of May (May 28 per text).
Gorbachev publicly announced Soviet troop withdrawal from Afghanistan.
Gandhi visited Washington, starting improved India-U.S. relations.
Pakistan Foreign Secretary Sattar visited India; no breakthrough.
Gandhi scheduled to return to Delhi from his trip.

key_claims: Gandhi told Dean that India was concerned over Zia's dismissal of Junejo and the setback to Pakistani democracy.
Gandhi argued US weapons aid to Pakistan lost justification once Soviets withdrew from Afghanistan.
Gandhi said India and the US share the goal of Soviet withdrawal but the future of Afghanistan should be left to Afghans.
The cable records Indian opposition to a Kabul government controlled by extremist fundamentalists such as Hekmatyar, while also not supporting Najibullah.
Gandhi linked Zia's Islamization and support for Afghan fundamentalists to a possible Islamic nuclear force and missile procurement.
India accuses Pakistan of continuing to aid terrorists in Punjab.
